name: Hesperidin
lead: Hesperidin is a flavanone glycoside found in citrus fruits, concentrated in the white inner peel; its aglycone is hesperetin.[1] It was first isolated in 1828 by the French chemist M. Lebreton.[1] It is sold as a dietary supplement, often combined with diosmin or vitamin C, in products aimed at venous and capillary complaints.[2][3]

People bring it into looks routines through the eye area and skin: the rationale offered is that capillary and venous support could reduce the swollen, discoloured look of under-eye puffiness, leg swelling or easy bruising. It is taken in citrus-bioflavonoid products and in diosmin combinations used for venous health.[2][3][4]

In appearance communities it is discussed in the context of puffiness, dark circles and visible or fragile blood vessels, based on the idea that it supports small blood vessels. No trial of hesperidin for periorbital puffiness or dark circles has been published; the clinical literature concerns venous, metabolic and other conditions, and Wikipedia describes research on hesperidin as preliminary, with reviews finding no clear effect on blood lipids or blood pressure and inconclusive results on endothelial function.[1]

angle.text: People use hesperidin, usually inside bioflavonoid or diosmin supplements, hoping to support small blood vessels and so reduce swelling, discolouration and bruising that show on the face and legs. The reasoning comes from its use in venous-health products.

infobox: Diosmin-hesperidin venous supplements; hesperidin methyl chalcone in bruising products[4][5]

paras: Hesperidin is named for the hesperidium, the type of fruit citrus trees bear.[1] It occurs in the white inner layer of citrus peel and in bitter orange, lemon, lime and orange juice; Wikipedia gives bitter orange fruit as containing roughly 700 to 2,500 ppm and lists dried peppermint (about 481 mg per 100 g) as richer than orange juice (about 26 mg per 100 ml).[1] In plants it is thought to contribute to defence, and it is made from L-phenylalanine in a nine-step route through the phenylpropanoid pathway.[1]

Citrus processing generates large amounts of peel and residue that are a source of hesperidin, which has driven research on extraction from juice by-products.[6] Some Ascomycete fungi carry an enzyme that splits hesperidin into hesperetin and rutinose, the same kind of sugar-removal step that gut bacteria perform in people.[1][7]

Lebreton isolated hesperidin from the white layer of citrus peel in 1828.[1] Hesperidin and related citrus flavonoids were later studied for effects on capillary strength; a 2001 review of its chemistry and pharmacology links dietary deficiency to capillary leakiness and extremity aches and notes no signs of toxicity at normal intakes.[8] A 2008 review describes much of the activity of citrus flavonoids as bearing on blood and microvascular endothelial cells, with epidemiological and animal data on cardiovascular protection.[9]

Hesperidin appears in supplements and creams marketed for tired-looking eyes, puffiness, visible capillaries and bruising. A US over-the-counter label for a bruising product lists hesperidin methyl chalcone among its citrus bioflavonoid ingredients alongside vitamin C, zinc, arnica and bromelain.[5]

Dark circles have several recognised causes, including thin lower-eyelid skin, superficial venous congestion, pigmentation, allergy-related rubbing, fatigue, ageing and nutritional factors, which is the setting in which vascular-support ingredients are discussed.[10]
Hesperidin is a component of citrus-flavonoid supplements for chronic venous insufficiency, haemorrhoids and capillary fragility, often paired with diosmin.[2][4]

Diosmin is a flavone glycoside made from citrus peel and sold as a non-prescription supplement in the United States and over the counter or by prescription in Europe (for example as Detralex).[4] Wikipedia describes moderate-quality evidence that diosmin and other phlebotonics improve leg and ankle swelling and lower-leg pain, and low-quality evidence for haemorrhoids.[4]

The same page reports about 10 percent of users with mild gastrointestinal upset or skin irritation, an undefined mechanism, an FDA conclusion in 2001 of inadequate evidence of safety that had not been revised by 2013, and a 2018 American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons listing of phlebotonics as a possible option for early-grade haemorrhoids.[4] Phlebotonics are not approved in Germany.[4] These findings concern diosmin-based venous products, not facial puffiness.

Laboratory and animal work describes antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity for hesperidin and hesperetin, including augmentation of cellular defences through the ERK/Nrf2 pathway.[11] Authors have proposed effects on capillary permeability and endothelial function, with human evidence limited.[1][8]

Hesperidin is poorly soluble and is absorbed mainly as hesperetin after gut bacteria remove the sugar group. A 2003 study measured human bioavailability of hesperidin and the related flavanone narirutin after two doses of orange juice.[7] A registered study compared the bioavailability of three hesperidin extracts.[12]

A 2001 review reports no signs of toxicity with normal intake of hesperidin or related compounds.[8] Mild gastrointestinal effects, headache and rash are occasionally reported with flavonoid supplements; diosmin-based products are reported to cause mild gastrointestinal or skin effects in around one in ten users.[4]
No studies found on hesperidin for facial puffiness, dark circles or other cosmetic outcomes.

Related research in other conditions: a 12-week open-label randomized trial of hesperidin, flaxseed and their combination in metabolic syndrome;[13] a controlled study of sulodexide and phlebotonic drugs in venous ulcers;[14] and older European trials of micronised flavonoid fractions in venous disease and in lymphoedema of the arm after breast cancer treatment.[15][16] A meta-analysis of 47 randomised trials examined dietary polyphenols in rheumatoid arthritis.[17] Wikipedia notes reviews from 2019 finding no effect on blood lipids or hypertension and inconclusive endothelial results.[1] Registered trials examine hesperidin for cognition in older adults, bone biomarkers in postmenopausal women, COVID-19 symptoms and metabolic syndrome.[18][19][20][21]

On T Nation, hesperidin mostly appears as an ingredient line in multivitamin and testosterone-booster formulas rather than as a stand-alone supplement. Posters list it within bioflavonoid complexes in multivitamins, with amounts in the low milligram range, and in a 'T booster' stack alongside quercetin.[22][23][24] One poster listed citrus flavonoids such as rutin and hesperidin as quercetin-related compounds in a diet post.[25] In a thread on burst blood vessels, a poster argued that a lack of flavonoids ('vitamin P') could leave vessels prone to rupture or leakage.[26]

lore.intro: In bodybuilding and supplement forums hesperidin is mainly discussed as part of bioflavonoid and multivitamin formulas and as a vessel-support nutrient.[22][26]

claims.claim: Flavonoids like hesperidin protect blood vessels from leaking or bursting
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says a lack of 'vitamin P' flavonoids leaves vessels prone to rupture and leakage.[26]
claims.experts: A 2001 review links dietary hesperidin deficiency to capillary leakiness and reports no toxicity at normal intake; a 2008 review says much citrus flavonoid activity concerns microvascular endothelial cells.[8][9]

claims.claim: Hesperidin supplements reduce under-eye puffiness or dark circles
claims.believers: Product copy and community discussion tie capillary support to a less swollen, less discoloured eye area.
claims.experts: No published trials test hesperidin for periorbital puffiness or dark circles; Wikipedia lists caffeine and vitamin C among topical ingredients discussed for dark circles.[10]

claims.claim: Hesperidin adds value inside a stack
claims.believers: Posters list it in multi-ingredient formulas next to quercetin and other flavonoids.[24]
claims.experts: Hesperidin is poorly soluble and absorbed largely as hesperetin after gut bacteria act on it; human absorption has been measured with orange juice.[7]
